newsitem.title: INDIA: India seen facing macro maze on convertible rupee.
newsitem.headline: India seen facing macro maze on convertible rupee.

text.p: India's plan for a fully convertible rupee by the turn of the century poses the problem of stopping an overvalued currency getting stronger, analysts said on Wednesday.
Rajan Govil, economist at HSBC B & K, reckons the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) will have to engineer a weaker rupee soon, helped by a slowdown in capital inflows.
"Exports were down 10 percent in April and and the strong rupee is a major reason," he said.
He expected the RBI to drag the rupee back to 37.8 to the dollar by March 1998, compared to Wednesday's rate of 35.77.
But India will pay for its more competitive exchange rate with higher inflation, Govil said.

A committee headed by former central bank governor S.S. Tarapore, which on Tuesday presented a report commissioned by Finance Minister P. Chidamabaram on how to make the rupee convertible on the capital account, was quite clear on the exchange rate risks involved.

"The international experience has shown that liberalisation of the capital account induces large capital inflows, which can cause a real appreciation of the exchange rate and erode the effectiveness of certain domestic macroeconomic policies," the report said.
The committee recommended that an inflation rate of three to five percent was one prerequisite for full convertibility.
It also said the Reserve Bank of India should be given more independence to pursue this goal.
Deregulation of interest rates and a reduction in banks' cash reserve ratio (CRR) to three percent by 1999/2000 from the current 9.5 percent were also on the committee's wish list.
Somehow the RBI must balance these goals with managing the exchange rate.

Most analysts reckon the rupee should be shedding three to five percent of its value annually, based on purchasing power parity criteria which take account of inflation differentials between India and major convertible currencies.
And Chidambaram, while leaving the RBI to do the job, said last month he would not like the rupee to strengthen further.
The RBI has intervened heavily to stop the rupee appreciating.

India's foreign exchange reserves, including gold and special drawing rights, have shot up to $27.79 billion, covering seven months' imports, from $21.6 billion a year ago -- which is a positive by-product for a country pursuing convertibility.
But the sale of rupees for dollars increases the domestic money supply, which will lead to inflation unless the RBI sterilises the surplus rupees through sales of government debt.
That is exactly what the RBI has done.
It has sold government paper covering around one-third of the central government's 1997/98 borrowing requirement in the first two months of the fiscal year.
Economists wonder what the RBI will do if the rupee is still straining at the leash at the end of the year, when there is little debt left to sell.
The authorities will be left with a stark choice of either letting the rupee rise or allowing inflation to rise, Sanjeev Sanyal, analyst at Bombay brokerage SocGen-Crosby, said.
"We're expecting the wholesale price index to average eight percent in 1997/98 against 6.4 percent last year," said HSBC's Govil. The WPI is running at 6.0 percent.
The Tarapore committee has pitched for an ideal, where all targets are achieved and the rupee can make a soft landing into the world of full convertibility.
But analysts are sceptical that the macroeconomic targets can be achieved.

A currency analyst at a major U.S. investment bank said India should press ahead with convertibility even if the targets are missed, as the markets could then force the monetary and fiscal discipline wherever the authorities fail.
"If you do not have a credible policy you should go ahead with capital convertibility because the markets will force one on you," he said.
The rupee has remained stubbornly strong, backed by heavy capital inflows, against the dollar, which itself is strong against other major currencies.
The U.S. banker said the rupee is currently overvalued by 10 percent on its real effective exchange rate index (REER) using 1993 as base year.
The Tarapore committee has recommended that the central bank try to hold the rupee in a plus or minus five percent band on its REER index.

It also said the index should be published to provide the market with a guide to the authorities' intentions. Currently, only an out of date REER index is published by the RBI, which releases the data infrequently.
"I think there is a real risk. You have to sterilise that intervention. The RBI has to resolve what it wants to target - money supply or REER," the U.S. investment banker said.
